records.name: Salesforce
records.oneLiner: Salesforce is a cloud-based AI CRM platform for sales, service, marketing, commerce, and related customer operations. ([salesforce.com](https://www.salesforce.com/?bc=OTH&lang=en&utm_source=openai))

auth.notes: Official Salesforce docs center API access on OAuth 2.0 flows. Supported flows documented by Salesforce include web server, device, JWT bearer, user-agent/hybrid, and username-password special scenarios; Salesforce also uses access tokens as bearer tokens for API requests. SOAP API login() is described in the integration guidance as legacy and supported until June 2027, so I am not treating it as the preferred path. ([help.salesforce.com](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_web_server_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5&utm_source=openai))

access.notes: The easiest path is a free Developer Edition org, which Salesforce says anyone can sign up for and which includes API access by default. For production orgs, API access is enabled by default in Enterprise, Unlimited, Performance, and Developer editions; Professional Edition requires the Web Services API add-on and account-executive involvement. A user also needs the API Enabled permission. ([trailhead.salesforce.com](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/environments-for-developers/explore-available-developer-environments?utm_source=openai))

api.notes: Salesforce publicly documents a wide API surface, including REST API, SOAP API, Bulk API 2.0, GraphQL API, Connect REST API, User Interface API, Tooling API, Metadata API, Streaming API, Pub/Sub API, and Apex custom web services. Salesforce states that programmatic access to org data includes SOAP, REST, and Bulk APIs, and that Platform Events and Streaming API are available in API-enabled editions. These surfaces support read/write integration overall, although some endpoints are specialized or partially read-oriented. ([help.salesforce.com](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=integrate_what_is_api.htm&language=en_US&utm_source=openai))

mcp.notes: Salesforce has official MCP support. Salesforce Help documents MCP Servers in API Catalog, and Salesforce’s hosted MCP servers GA announcement says MCP-compatible clients can connect to Salesforce orgs using the open MCP standard with standard OAuth authentication. Salesforce also says it includes a native MCP client for agents. ([help.salesforce.com](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.api_catalog_manage_mcp_servers.htm&language=en_US&type=5&utm_source=openai))

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: HubSpot
records.oneLiner: HubSpot is a CRM platform for managing customer records, deals, sales processes, and related customer data, with free CRM tools and paid hub tiers.

auth.notes: Official HubSpot docs describe OAuth for multi-account/public apps and static auth access tokens for single-account installs. HubSpot also documents legacy private app access tokens and service keys as bearer-token-style credentials for API access. Legacy developer API keys are documented for a small set of app features/endpoints and are separate from API access; HubSpot has also announced API key sunset. I therefore treat OAuth, private/static bearer tokens, and service keys as supported API auth methods, while legacy API keys are legacy and limited.

access.notes: HubSpot offers free CRM tools with no credit card required, up to 2 users, and 1,000 contacts; paid tiers are also available. For app-style access, OAuth installs for multi-account apps require the installing user to have permission for requested scopes, and if not, the app may need a Super Admin to install it. Private/static auth is limited to a single authorized account. Service Keys require Developer Tools access and can only be granted scopes the creator already has.

api.notes: HubSpot exposes broad REST APIs across CRM objects and related activities. The object APIs support create, retrieve, update, upsert, associations, pin activity, and delete for supported objects. Official docs list many standard objects such as contacts, companies, deals, tickets, products, quotes, invoices, orders, tasks, notes, meetings, emails, calls, line items, subscriptions, and custom objects, indicating broad CRM coverage. Many endpoints are read/write, though some objects have limited functionality and access depends on scopes and account permissions.

mcp.notes: HubSpot has an official remote MCP server at mcp.hubspot.com. Official docs say it is separate from the developer MCP server and is intended for CRM data access. It supports read and write actions, uses OAuth with PKCE via MCP auth apps, and is generally available according to HubSpot’s official pages/changelog.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: Pipedrive
records.oneLiner: A web-based sales CRM for tracking leads, deals, contacts, pipelines, and sales activity.

auth.notes: Official docs say the REST API validates requests against an API token that can be obtained manually from the Pipedrive app. Pipedrive also supports OAuth 2.0 for apps in the Marketplace; OAuth flows exchange authorization codes for access/refresh tokens, and the access token is used to access user data through the API. The OAuth token endpoint uses HTTP Basic auth with client_id/client_secret during token exchange, but that is app-client authentication rather than a user access method. Pipedrive also says API access can be revoked for global regular users via permissions.

access.notes: Pipedrive offers a free 14-day trial with full access and no credit card required. The API key is included free with every Pipedrive subscription, and the trial page indicates full product access during trial. By default, all users in a company can access their own API token, but an admin can revoke API token access for global regular users via permission sets. I therefore treat the easiest credential path as self-serve, with admin permission gating for some users.

api.notes: Pipedrive exposes a RESTful API with JSON output, OpenAPI 3 specs for v1 and v2, Postman/Insomnia support, and official Node.js and PHP client libraries. The documented endpoint list spans core CRM objects such as activities, deals, leads, organizations, persons, pipelines, products, projects, notes, users, roles, and webhooks. The API reference explicitly says the API and extension points cover the majority of core product functionality. Webhooks are also available for push notifications on create/change/delete events.

mcp.notes: Pipedrive has an official native MCP offering documented in the Help Center and a Claude connector pointing to the official MCP endpoint at mcp.pipedrive.ai/mcp. Pipedrive also has community MCP implementations discussed in the Pipedrive Developers' Community, so MCP coverage is not official-only. The official MCP tools article shows read/search/create/update actions for activities, deals, persons, organizations, leads, pipeline stages, and notes.

buildability.rationale: No useful documented public agent-callable surface was verified.

records.name: Attio
records.oneLiner: A customizable CRM platform for managing people, companies, deals, tasks, notes, and related sales/workflow data.

auth.notes: For the REST API, Attio officially supports OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow and single-workspace API keys. Both are used as bearer tokens in the Authorization header, and Attio also supports HTTP Basic authentication with the token as username and a blank password. For MCP, Attio uses OAuth authentication. Attio also exposes an app/server token for Attio apps, but that is an app-internal server token rather than a separate end-user auth method, so I did not count it as a distinct credential path.

access.notes: Attio offers a free plan and a 14-day Pro trial with no credit card required, and the API docs say single-workspace API keys can be generated from developer settings. MCP is available on all plans and all workspace members. I do not see evidence of a required paid gate for basic API access.

api.notes: Attio provides a public REST API over HTTPS, plus an App SDK and webhooks. The REST API supports broad workspace operations across objects, lists, records, notes, tasks, threads, comments, meetings, call recordings, transcripts, files, webhooks, and meta endpoints; standard objects include people, companies, and deals, with support for custom objects and lists. The docs explicitly describe the REST API as able to read and write information to and from Attio workspaces. Attio MCP is a hosted MCP server for AI tools that can search, read, create, and update CRM data; Attio’s MCP page also states read operations are auto-approved and write operations require confirmation.

mcp.notes: Official hosted MCP exists at mcp.attio.com/mcp. Attio’s help center says it is available on all plans and all workspace members, uses OAuth, and supports AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, and other MCP-compatible clients. I did not find evidence of a separate community MCP for Attio.

records.name: Twenty
records.oneLiner: Open-source CRM for building customizable sales workflows, objects, views, automations, and AI-assisted CRM experiences.

auth.notes: For public API access, Twenty documents API-key auth via `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY`, created in Settings → APIs & Webhooks → + Create key. For OAuth, Twenty supports authorization code + PKCE for user-facing apps and client credentials for server-to-server access, with dynamic client registration. OAuth scopes include `api` (full read/write access to Core and Metadata APIs) and `profile`. Cloud/hosted OAuth endpoints are documented at `https://api.twenty.com`, while self-hosted uses the instance domain. I did not find evidence for any other public API auth method beyond API key and OAuth2, so I am not inferring more.

access.notes: Twenty is self-serve: users can sign up on the cloud and pick a 30-day trial (with card) or 7-day trial (without card), and both include full access including API. Twenty also offers a free self-hosted plan with all Pro features at no cost. The Cloud Pro plan and Organization plan are paid tiers; Organization adds premium features like SSO and row-level permissions. For the easiest no-infrastructure path, the cloud trial is the lowest-friction route; for fully free access, self-hosted is available if you are willing to run the stack yourself.

api.notes: Twenty exposes two public API surfaces: Core API and Metadata API. The docs state both are available as REST and GraphQL. Core API covers CRUD for records such as people, companies, opportunities, and custom objects, plus querying/filtering/relationship traversal. Metadata API lets you create/modify/delete objects, fields, and relations, so it can change the data model programmatically. Docs also mention batch operations up to 60 records per request and 100 requests per minute. The repository and docs also reference SDK/app extensibility, but the load-bearing public agent-callable surfaces are the REST/GraphQL APIs plus the native MCP surface.

mcp.notes: Official Twenty sources state that every Cloud workspace ships with a native MCP server, and the product site says AI assistants can connect via OAuth and read/write CRM data. The release notes also describe AI agents, chats, and MCP support. I did not verify a separate community MCP as an official capability, so I am marking community MCP as not found.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: Slack
records.oneLiner: Slack is a workplace communications platform, and its developer platform lets apps and agents read, write, and react inside Slack workspaces.

auth.notes: Slack apps use OAuth 2.0 installation flows to obtain access tokens. Those tokens are then sent as bearer tokens to the Web API. Slack’s token model includes bot tokens, user tokens, app-level tokens, workflow tokens, configuration tokens, and service tokens, but the general app- and agent-facing credential path is OAuth 2.0 plus bearer-token API calls. Sign in with Slack is a separate OpenID Connect login flow, not the primary app-access path.

access.notes: Basic app creation and installation are self-serve: create a Slack app, request scopes, and install it to a workspace. Slack’s docs also describe free workspaces and a free developer sandbox. Enterprise/org-level scopes and some distribution cases require public distribution and admin-approved installation paths. For MCP, Slack currently restricts usage to internal apps and marketplace-published apps.

api.notes: Slack’s public agent-callable surface is broad: the Web API has over 100 HTTP RPC-style methods; the Events API delivers activity callbacks; Socket Mode can replace a public request URL; incoming webhooks can post messages; slash commands, shortcuts, and interactive Block Kit components provide user-invoked entry points; and the Slack MCP server exposes AI-oriented tools for search, reading, and actions. Much of the platform is read/write, including message posting, conversation management, and interactive actions.

mcp.notes: Slack has an official MCP server and official Slackbot MCP client documentation. The official docs say the Slack MCP server can search Slack, retrieve and send messages, manage canvases, and access member info. Slack also states that only internal apps or Slack Marketplace-published apps may use MCP; unlisted apps are prohibited.

records.name: Lark (Larksuite)
records.oneLiner: Lark’s developer/open platform for building bots, web apps, blocks, and integrations on top of its communications, messaging, and broader workplace APIs.

auth.notes: Official API docs show requests authenticated with Bearer access tokens, including tenant_access_token for app identity and user_access_token for logged-in-user identity. The official MCP project also supports OAuth-based user login for user identity. I did not find official evidence of api_key, basic, personal_token, service_account, or other distinct auth modes for this platform.

access.notes: The Open Platform is publicly self-serve from the developer console/open platform. Official server API docs state core auth/authorization, event subscription, and contacts are free regardless of plan, while many basic APIs are plan-tallied and advanced APIs require a dedicated quota package. So the easiest credential path is to create an app in the developer console and obtain an app credential, then use tenant_access_token; some surfaces also allow user_access_token after OAuth login. If you need advanced APIs, access becomes paid/quota-gated.

api.notes: Official docs describe 2500+ APIs across many product areas. For communications/messaging specifically, the server API list includes send, reply, edit, forward, recall, read-status queries, chat history, and message resource download; contacts APIs are also available. The platform supports server-side REST APIs, SDKs, event subscription/webhooks, and client APIs inside Lark apps. Messaging APIs are read/write overall, with some endpoints being read-only.

mcp.notes: Official GitHub repository larksuite/lark-openapi-mcp exposes Lark Open Platform APIs as MCP tools. It supports both app-identity mode and OAuth user-identity mode, using the open.larksuite.com domain. I did not find separate community MCP evidence that was stronger than the official repo.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: Pumble
records.oneLiner: A team chat and collaboration app for channels, direct messages, file sharing, calls, and workspace messaging.

auth.notes: Pumble’s public agent-callable surfaces are primarily the API addon, incoming webhooks, and the official MCP server. The API addon uses a generated API key entered in Swagger/Authorize after installing the addon. The MCP server requires an app key plus user/bot token headers. Incoming webhooks use a unique per-webhook URL. I found no official evidence of OAuth/basic/bearer auth for the public API surfaces, so I am not claiming them.

access.notes: Public integration access is self-serve and available on all plans. The API addon is available to Owner/Admin/Member. Addons can be installed by admins/workspace owners; once installed, members can authorize/use them, except single-channel and multi-channel guests. Free workspaces allow up to 3 addons; Pro up to 10; Business/Enterprise unlimited. Pumble also offers a free plan and free incoming webhooks.

api.notes: REST-like public surface: the API addon exposes actions such as sending messages, replying, deleting messages, reacting, creating channels, and listing messages/channels/DMs. Incoming webhooks are write-only message posting via HTTP POST to a unique URL. The official MCP server exposes a dynamic tool set driven by selected user/bot scopes, including read tools (search/get/list/fetch) and write tools (send/edit/delete/react/create/schedule). Overall breadth is moderate rather than broad because the public surfaces are scoped to messaging and workspace collaboration, not a full admin/developer platform API.

mcp.notes: Official Pumble help documents a hosted MCP endpoint at mcp.pumble.com/mcp and lists official tools/prompt helpers. I found no evidence of a separate community MCP implementation.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: Discord
records.oneLiner: A communications and messaging platform whose developer platform lets apps, bots, and integrations interact with servers, channels, messages, and users.

auth.notes: Official docs say Discord API authentication is done with either a bot token or an OAuth2 bearer token. Bot users are created in the Developer Portal and generate a bot token; that token is then sent as `Authorization: Bot <token>`. Discord also supports OAuth2 flows for user- or app-authorized access, including authorization code, implicit, and client credentials. The OAuth2 token exchange for client credentials uses HTTP Basic authentication with client id and client secret.

access.notes: Creating a Discord application is self-serve in the Developer Portal. Basic bot/app development is available without approval, but some capabilities are gated: discovery requires app verification, and verified apps need approval for privileged intents. Monetization and discovery are also separately gated by verification. I did not find a pricing page indicating a paid developer tier for core app access.

api.notes: Discord exposes a broad public REST API as the primary programmatic surface, plus Gateway-based real-time events and HTTP interactions for commands, buttons, modals, and other interactive features. Docs also describe RPC for local client integration and webhooks as part of the broader platform. For agent-callable server-side integration, the public surface is broad and supports both reading and writing across messages, guilds/servers, channels, commands, and interactions, subject to scopes, permissions, and intents.

mcp.notes: Discord’s official docs site itself now has MCP support for documentation access, including an official docs MCP endpoint mentioned in the changelog. I did not find evidence of an official Discord platform MCP server for bot/app operations. I did find community Discord MCP servers in GitHub search results, so community MCP exists, but it is distinct from Discord’s official docs MCP support.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

auth.notes: Official docs say SendGrid supports API keys and recommends them as the preferred way to authenticate. For Web API v3, requests use an Authorization header with Bearer <API key>. For SMTP relay, docs say to use username 'apikey' and the API key as the password; the authentication page also describes this as basic authentication using an API key. Official docs also note that basic authentication with a username/password is no longer accepted for the API itself.

access.notes: As of 2025, new accounts created directly through sendgrid.com or twilio.com receive a 60-day timed free trial with access to both Email API and Marketing Campaigns, capped at 100 emails/day for each area and 100 Marketing contacts. After trial expiration, sending stops unless the account upgrades to a paid Email API and/or Marketing Campaigns plan. SendGrid also offers self-serve pricing with a 'Start for free' path and paid tiers; some higher-volume or enterprise options require contact sales.

api.notes: The public agent-callable surface is broad: the Twilio SendGrid v3 Web API is REST-based and covers mail send, campaigns, single sends, contacts, statistics, IP management, subusers, templates, and related account features. Official docs also provide SDKs/libraries for multiple languages and support webhooks such as Event Webhook; SMTP relay is also documented for sending. The surface is read-write, since it supports creating, updating, deleting, scheduling, and sending across marketing and email resources.

mcp.notes: No official SendGrid-specific MCP server or community MCP integration was found in official SendGrid/Twilio sources during this review. Twilio has a separate general MCP page that mentions SendGrid docs/support articles, but that is not a SendGrid MCP integration.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: Shopify
records.oneLiner: An ecommerce platform and developer platform for building online stores, storefront experiences, and merchant/admin integrations.

auth.notes: Official docs support OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant for public/standalone apps, token exchange for embedded/admin apps, and access-token-based auth for admin-created custom apps. Storefront API also supports tokenless access plus token-based access via public/private storefront access tokens. Shopify also documents HTTP Basic auth for the Shop Partners API. Client credentials grant is documented for apps built for an organization without user interaction.

access.notes: Core developer access is self-serve through the Dev Dashboard/Shopify CLI. Dev stores are free and available to Shopify Partners with app development permissions. Public app distribution can require app review, but basic API/app development does not require sales or partner approval. Some store-level actions still require store owner/staff/collaborator permissions.

api.notes: Shopify exposes broad commerce APIs, including the GraphQL Admin API, legacy REST Admin API, Storefront API, official SDKs/client libraries, and UCP-compliant MCP endpoints for agentic commerce. The REST Admin API is legacy as of Oct 1, 2024, and new public apps should use GraphQL Admin API. Storefront API includes tokenless read/write cart operations plus token-based access for broader features.

mcp.notes: Official MCP coverage exists. Shopify documents Storefront MCP, Storefront Catalog MCP, Cart MCP, Checkout MCP, Order MCP, and WebMCP tools on storefronts. No community MCP evidence was used or found in this pass.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: WooCommerce
records.oneLiner: A free, open-source WordPress ecommerce platform whose REST API lets external systems create, read, update, and delete store data; WooCommerce also exposes an MCP endpoint for AI assistants. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/pricing/))

auth.notes: Official docs say WooCommerce REST API keys are generated in WooCommerce admin or via the app authentication endpoint. For REST calls over HTTPS, the docs and examples use consumer key/secret with Basic Auth; for HTTP, WooCommerce recommends OAuth 1.0a one-legged signing. The app-auth endpoint `/wc-auth/v1/authorize` is only for generating API keys for an application, not for customer login. ([developer.woocommerce.com](https://developer.woocommerce.com/docs/apis/rest-api/authentication/))

access.notes: WooCommerce describes itself as a free, open-source ecommerce platform with no platform fees or revenue share, and the free core includes unlimited products, orders, and APIs. The REST API requires WooCommerce 3.5+, WordPress 4.4+, and pretty permalinks. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/pricing/))

api.notes: The current REST integration is v3 at `/wp-json/wc/v3/`, with JSON over standard HTTP verbs. Official docs say WC data can be created, read, updated, and deleted; the API reference covers resources such as orders, products, coupons, customers, order actions, and order notes. The MCP docs say WooCommerce also ships an MCP endpoint at `/wp-json/woocommerce/mcp`, with tool packs for orders, products, customers, coupons, refunds, tax, shipping, webhooks, reports, and more. ([developer.woocommerce.com](https://developer.woocommerce.com/docs/apis/rest-api/))

mcp.notes: Official WooCommerce docs describe a built-in WooCommerce MCP endpoint at `/wp-json/woocommerce/mcp`, enabled by the MCP for WooCommerce plugin, which is presented as configuring/extending the official integration. The docs also state the connector uses API keys and tool-pack gating. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/document/w7s-mcp/))

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: BigCommerce
records.oneLiner: An ecommerce platform with APIs for store management, storefront/headless commerce, customer authentication, checkout, webhooks, and AI-agent storefront tools.

auth.notes: Primary developer path is OAuth-based API accounts. BigCommerce documents store-level, app-level, and account-level OAuth API accounts; most REST Admin and GraphQL Admin APIs use X-Auth-Token with an access token. GraphQL Storefront API uses Bearer tokens. BigCommerce also documents same-origin CORS access for REST Storefront APIs, Basic auth for Tax Provider APIs, and developer-defined request-body keys for Shipping Provider APIs. Legacy HTTP Basic for API accounts is noted as no longer available to new stores.

access.notes: Store owners or authorized users can create store-level API accounts in the control panel without a sales-led process. App-level API accounts can be created in the Developer Portal. Public marketplace distribution adds approval gating: BigCommerce notes that apps submitted for public listing require Marketplace approval, and public apps can generate access tokens on behalf of store owners once approved. BigCommerce also offers a public free trial and subscription plans, but API credential creation itself is largely self-serve once you have a store/account.

api.notes: BigCommerce exposes REST Admin APIs, REST Storefront APIs, GraphQL Storefront API, GraphQL Account API, Customer Login API, Current Customer API, Payments-related endpoints, webhooks, and provider APIs. Official docs describe store management, catalog, checkout, customer identity, headless storefront, and payment flows. Agent-callable surfaces include storefront search/cart/checkout MCP tools and checkout URL flows. Most Admin/management APIs are read-write; storefront APIs include both read and write operations for carts and checkout, and some storefront endpoints are read-only or browser-context only.

mcp.notes: Official MCP support is documented under BigCommerce Docs for B2C Storefront. The B2C storefront MCP server supports guest shopping flows and includes tools for searching products, managing carts, and creating checkout URLs. The docs also reference mcp as a supported order_source in checkout URLs.

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: Salesforce Commerce Cloud
records.oneLiner: Salesforce’s B2C e-commerce platform for building storefronts and managing shopper, catalog, order, inventory, and custom commerce APIs.

auth.notes: Official docs split access into Shopper APIs and Admin APIs. Shopper APIs use SLAS (OAuth 2.1) and JWT bearer tokens; Admin APIs use Account Manager OAuth with a JWT bearer token. Custom APIs can be secured with ShopperToken or AmOAuth2 schemes, which reuse the same underlying auth families. The documented fastest path for a shopper token is to create a SLAS client and call /token; for an admin token, create an API client in Account Manager and POST to oauth2/access_token.

access.notes: Salesforce’s public pricing page lists B2C Commerce editions as contact for pricing. Developer docs also indicate production use typically requires an existing B2C Commerce instance or on-demand sandboxes, and on-demand sandboxes require purchased credits plus role and client setup. There is no public self-serve trial documented for full production access.

api.notes: SCAPI is the main public API surface and is divided into Shopper APIs and Admin APIs. Shopper APIs are customer-facing and mostly read-only, with exceptions such as baskets and orders; Admin APIs are merchant-facing and read/write. Salesforce also documents Custom APIs under the SCAPI framework, plus SDKs, Postman collections, and a B2C DX MCP Server that can discover SCAPI schemas, scaffold custom endpoints, deploy cartridges, and work with MRT.

mcp.notes: Salesforce documents an official B2C DX MCP Server implemented in @salesforce/b2c-dx-mcp. The docs describe it as a developer-preview unified MCP server for B2C Commerce, with tools for SCAPI discovery, custom API scaffolding, cartridges, Storefront Next, PWA Kit v3, MRT, and diagnostics. I found no official evidence of a separate community MCP server for this product.

buildability.rationale: The API exists, but production credentials require vendor outreach or approval.

records.name: Magento (Adobe Commerce)
records.oneLiner: An enterprise ecommerce platform for building and operating B2C/B2B storefronts and commerce integrations, with REST and GraphQL web APIs plus extensibility tooling.

auth.notes: Official docs show three core auth paths: legacy PaaS integrations use OAuth 1.0a for third-party applications; Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service uses Adobe IMS via OAuth 2.0 for server-to-server and user-based flows; GraphQL and REST calls are then authorized with Bearer tokens/authorization tokens. Browser/session-cookie auth is also supported for GraphQL, but Adobe recommends tokens instead. The enum cannot express OAuth 1.0a directly, so it is represented here as custom.

access.notes: Adobe Commerce pricing is customized and the product pages direct buyers to 'Get pricing' / 'Contact us'. The onboarding docs state that if you do not have an Adobe Commerce on cloud infrastructure account, you must contact Sales. Magento Open Source is separately described as free/open source, but that is a different product line from Adobe Commerce.

api.notes: Public agent-callable surfaces include the Commerce Web APIs (REST and GraphQL), with REST reference coverage for the full endpoint set and GraphQL support for customer/admin actions. Adobe also documents event-driven extensibility and webhooks/App Builder patterns, which are relevant public integration surfaces. REST covers many commerce operations, and GraphQL supports authenticated customer/admin mutations as well as queries.

mcp.notes: Adobe documents an official Commerce development MCP server as part of the Commerce development MCPs and skills, and also documents the @dropins/mcp server for storefront development. I did not find evidence of a community MCP specifically for Adobe Commerce/Magento in the official research pass.

buildability.rationale: The API exists, but production credentials require vendor outreach or approval.

records.name: Squarespace
records.oneLiner: Squarespace is a website and ecommerce platform whose developer APIs let apps manage merchant-site commerce data such as products, orders, inventory, contacts, discounts, webhooks, and related site metadata.

auth.notes: Official docs say Commerce APIs accept either a generated API key or an OAuth access token. API keys are created from the site’s Developer API Keys panel; the key is shown once and does not expire while the merchant site remains active. OAuth is used for Squarespace Extensions and requires registering as an OAuth client, then authorizing via the OAuth flow. I did not find any official support for basic auth, personal tokens, service accounts, or a standalone bearer-token method beyond using the API key or OAuth token in the Authorization: Bearer header.

access.notes: For the easiest credential path, a merchant can self-serve an API key, but official docs limit custom applications with API keys to the Commerce Advanced plan. OAuth can be used for Squarespace Extensions, and the developer portal says extensions are available to customers on any plan, but obtaining OAuth credentials requires registering as an OAuth client via Squarespace’s process. The least-gated path for raw API access is therefore self-serve paid; the least-gated path for extension-style integration is self-serve on any plan with OAuth registration/authorization.

api.notes: Squarespace’s public commerce surface is primarily REST APIs. Official docs expose a broad set of agent-callable endpoints including Authorization/Website, Website, Products, Orders, Inventory, Contacts, Discounts, Transactions, Analytics, Profiles, and Webhook Subscriptions. Many resources support both read and write operations; some are read-only, and webhook subscriptions are OAuth-only. The Website API and Authorization API are read-only; Products, Orders, Inventory, Contacts, Discounts, and Webhook Subscriptions include write-capable operations; Analytics and Transactions are read-only.

mcp.notes: I found no official MCP server or official/community MCP listing for Squarespace in the searched official sources.

buildability.rationale: The API is buildable, but obtaining credentials requires a paid plan.

records.name: Gumroad
records.oneLiner: An ecommerce platform for creators to sell digital products, memberships/subscriptions, and software access from their own Gumroad storefronts.

auth.notes: Official docs describe two API paths: a manual access-token flow for your own Gumroad account, and an OAuth2 flow (“Sign in with Gumroad”) for any account. auth.notes: For database-facing public surfaces, Neo4j documents Basic auth for username/password access to the Query API and MCP server, and Bearer token auth when integrating with SSO/OIDC/OAuth-backed identities. records.name: Snowflake
records.oneLiner: Cloud data platform for storage, SQL analytics, data engineering, application development, and AI/agent workloads.

auth.notes: Official docs show multiple auth families across Snowflake surfaces. For end-user sign-in to Snowsight, Snowflake documents SSO and username/password with MFA. For applications and APIs, Snowflake documents Snowflake OAuth, External OAuth, key-pair authentication, programmatic access tokens (PATs), and workload identity federation; Snowflake REST APIs specifically accept key-pair JWT, OAuth, and PATs, and Snowflake-managed MCP servers default to Snowflake OAuth with optional External OAuth. I mapped api_key to key-pair because it is the clearest self-serve credential path in the docs, but Snowflake’s docs do not use the term api_key directly. access.notes: Snowflake offers a self-service free trial: only a valid email address is required, no payment information, and the trial lasts 30 days or until free usage is exhausted. api.notes: Snowflake has broad public programmatic surfaces: Snowflake REST APIs, Snowflake SQL API, Snowflake Python APIs, the Python Connector/driver surface, and Snowflake-managed MCP servers. The managed MCP server can expose Cortex Analyst, Cortex Search, Cortex Agents, custom tools, and SQL executions on the standards-based interface; MCP clients discover and invoke tools via tools/list and tools/call. records.name: MongoDB Atlas
records.oneLiner: MongoDB’s hosted database platform and management plane for provisioning, configuring, and operating MongoDB deployments in the cloud.

auth.notes: For the Atlas Administration API, MongoDB documents two authentication methods: Digest auth using an Authorization header token and service accounts using OAuth2 client credentials. MongoDB recommends service accounts over API keys, and also says API keys are a legacy authentication method. For Atlas MCP Atlas tools, the MCP server requires Atlas API credentials, specifically an API client ID and API client secret; this is effectively the service-account/OAuth2 path. Atlas also documents broader Atlas authentication guidance across UI, database, and API, including federated auth for UI and development-time options like SCRAM/X.509 for database access, but those are not the documented Atlas Administration API auth methods.

access.notes: Atlas offers a self-serve free cluster tier, which can be created via UI, CLI, or the Atlas Administration API. However, programmatic access to Atlas resources is role-gated: creating/managing programmatic access at the organization level requires Organization Owner access, and API capabilities follow Atlas user roles. The API can also be restricted by an API access list, and each authentication method has its own access list. Paid clusters unlock full Atlas functionality, while free clusters provide only a subset of features.

api.notes: The Atlas Administration API is a versioned REST API with JSON entities, HTTPS-only transport, and support for common HTTP methods including GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, and HEAD. MongoDB also provides an Atlas CLI wrapper over the API. The public agent-callable surface is broad because Atlas tools can manage organizations, projects, clusters, database users, access settings, and related operations.

mcp.notes: MongoDB documents an official MongoDB MCP Server. Its Atlas tools are official and available only when Atlas API credentials are configured. Documented Atlas tools include list/create orgs and projects, list/inspect/create/upgrade/connect clusters, and create free clusters. The server can also create a temporary database user when connecting without a stored connection string. No separate community Atlas MCP was found in official research.

records.name: Sentry
records.oneLiner: Developer monitoring platform for errors, performance, traces, profiling, logs, releases, and related workflow data, with a public web API for managing organizations, projects, teams, integrations, and event data.

auth.notes: Official docs describe four concrete API auth paths: org/internal-integration auth tokens sent as `Authorization: Bearer ...`; user personal tokens for user-scoped endpoints; OAuth2 authorization-code flow for third-party apps; legacy API keys via HTTP Basic auth. Docs also mention DSN-based auth for a small number of endpoints, but that is limited and endpoint-specific, so I have not treated it as a general supported API auth method for the platform API. Creating organization auth tokens through an internal integration requires an org-level Manager or Admin role; user personal tokens are created in User settings > Personal Tokens. OAuth2 is available for apps acting on behalf of users, but OAuth alone does not imply self-service access to all API surfaces.

access.notes: Sentry documents a free Developer plan and recommends it for API tutorials; some workflows require higher org roles. For organizational auth tokens created through internal integrations, the tutorial states a Manager or Admin role is required. There is also a paid subscription/billing experience, but the docs I found do not make the API itself paid-only. Overall, the platform is self-serve, with some token-creation and feature workflows gated by role or plan.

api.notes: The public Sentry web API is REST-style and documented as versioned v0. It supports account-level resources like organizations and teams, plus data management/export. Official docs show readable/writable endpoints across organizations, teams, projects, integrations, traces, profiling, attachments, SCIM, and user/org endpoints. Examples include GET/POST/PUT/DELETE endpoints for orgs, projects, teams, integrations, and SCIM, so the public API is clearly read-write rather than read-only. The docs also note some endpoints are beta and subject to change.

mcp.notes: I found no official Sentry MCP documentation or official MCP product page in the searched docs/changelog. I also found no clear community MCP repository in official Sentry sources. There is an official Sentry SDK changelog note mentioning 'MCP SDK v2 handler signature is now supported in the MCP integration,' which indicates internal SDK integration support for MCP-related instrumentation, but not a documented public MCP server or agent-facing MCP endpoint.

auth.notes: For the public Web API, Airtable’s current supported auth is Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and OAuth tokens. records.name: Plaid
records.oneLiner: Plaid is a financial data platform and API that lets apps connect to users’ financial accounts, access bank-account and identity data, and support payments/funding workflows.

auth.notes: For the main Plaid API, Plaid issues a live `client_id` and `secret` via the Dashboard after signup and terms acceptance; almost all API endpoints require those credentials, sent either in the request body or as `PLAID-CLIENT-ID` and `PLAID-SECRET`. For the Dashboard MCP server, Plaid uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials to mint an `access_token`, which is then sent as a Bearer token. OAuth in Link is for end-user institution auth, not the developer’s Plaid API credential path. ([plaid.com](https://plaid.com/docs/api/))

access.notes: Plaid’s docs say you create a Dashboard account to get API access and keys. Pricing docs say Trial plans are free, require a Dashboard account and email verification, and new trial teams can access production data with a 10-Item limit; Production access is requested through the Dashboard. Some pricing tiers and certain products require paid plans or sales contact. ([plaid.com](https://plaid.com/docs/api/))

api.notes: Plaid’s API reference is a comprehensive reference for endpoints and webhooks, served over HTTPS as JSON over HTTP. The docs and home page show many product areas and endpoints across Auth, Balance, Identity, Link, Users, and more, indicating broad surface area. The API includes read endpoints like `/accounts/get` and `/identity/get`, as well as write/setup endpoints like `/link/token/create`, `/item/remove`, and `/user/create`. ([plaid.com](https://plaid.com/docs/api/))

mcp.notes: Plaid officially offers a Dashboard MCP server at `https://api.dashboard.plaid.com/mcp/`. It is remote MCP over Streamable HTTP, requires Production access, and is limited to dashboard diagnostics/analytics tools such as item debugging, Link analytics, usage metrics, and team listing. Plaid also mentions a local AI coding toolkit MCP server, but that is a developer utility rather than the Dashboard server. ([plaid.com](https://plaid.com/docs/resources/mcp/))

buildability.rationale: A useful public surface and a self-serve credential path are both available.

records.name: Binance
records.oneLiner: A cryptocurrency exchange and financial platform whose developer docs expose APIs for market data, account operations, trading, streaming, and related institutional workflows.

auth.notes: Official docs say many private endpoints require authentication and that API keys are created in Binance account API Management. Supported auth mechanisms include HMAC-based request signing, asymmetric key authentication (RSA and Ed25519), and session-based authentication for selected WebSocket and FIX workflows. The key is typically sent as `X-MBX-APIKEY` for signed REST requests, with a request signature added for secure endpoints.

access.notes: The API is self-serve from a Binance account via API Management; the docs do not indicate required paid developer tiers for basic API access. For Spot REST, public market-data endpoints are available without credentials, while secure endpoints require an API key and permission enablement. Trading permission must be enabled in API Management for TRADE endpoints.

api.notes: Official docs describe REST, WebSocket APIs, WebSocket Streams, FIX APIs, and SBE, with product coverage spanning Spot, Futures, Margin, Wallet, Convert, Portfolio Margin, Algo Trading, Copy Trading, Sub Account, VIP Service, and more. For agent-callable public surfaces, the docs explicitly mention an Agent REST API and document product APIs for both public market data and private account/trading actions. The Spot REST reference states security types NONE, TRADE, USER_DATA, and USER_STREAM; NONE is public market data, TRADE is order placement/cancellation, USER_DATA is private account data, and USER_STREAM manages user data stream subscriptions.

mcp.notes: Binance’s official developer docs explicitly list an MCP Server under Agent Native and describe it as a Model Context Protocol server for AI development tools. I did not find evidence of a separate community MCP implementation in the sources reviewed.

buildability.rationale: No useful documented public agent-callable surface was verified.

records.name: QuickBooks

identity.officialName: QuickBooks Online Accounting API (QuickBooks / Intuit Developer Platform)

records.oneLiner: A cloud accounting and bookkeeping platform whose developer API lets apps read and write core business data such as customers, invoices, bills, payments, reports, and related accounting entities in QuickBooks Online.

auth.notes: Official QuickBooks Online API access is through Intuit OAuth 2.0: apps create an Intuit Developer app, get a Client ID and Client Secret, send users through consent, exchange the authorization code for access and refresh tokens, and send requests with the bearer access token. The docs also describe OpenID Connect for Intuit single sign-on, but that is a sign-in model for users, not a separate public API credential type. I found no official evidence of API key, basic auth, personal token, service account, or custom credential auth for the QuickBooks Online API.

access.notes: A developer profile automatically gets a sandbox company, so there is self-serve free sandbox access for development. Production access requires a registered Intuit app and user consent. The current partner program is the main gating layer for premium APIs: Builder tier is automatic and uncharged, while Silver/Gold/Platinum are paid tiers with premium API access; premium APIs are only available to Silver, Gold, and Platinum partners.

api.notes: The QuickBooks Online Accounting API supports REST and GraphQL, with official docs saying apps can create, read, update, query, and send entities such as invoices, and can work with many customer-facing accounting resources including customers, vendors, employees, invoices, bills, payments, refunds, reports, and more. The API Explorer documents entity-level operations. Some premium APIs are restricted to higher partner tiers.

mcp.notes: I found no official Intuit MCP server or MCP documentation for QuickBooks on the official developer domain. I also did not find a community MCP result in this research pass. As of today, none found.

buildability.rationale: The API is buildable, but obtaining credentials requires a paid plan.
